newsitem.title: USA: U.S. West spot power down as weather warms up.
newsitem.headline: U.S. West spot power down as weather warms up.

text.p: Spot power prices during peak demand hours in the western U.S. continued to fall amid warmer weather and plentiful hydroelectric supplies, market sources said Thursday.
"Prices started in the low $30s (per megawatt hour), but they came down pretty quickly," said one trader.
"Temperatures are warming up and some people have a lot of water to move," said another market source.

Through the weekend, temperatures in the Pacific Northwest are expected to run slightly above normal, with normal to above-normal temperatures forecast for the next 6 to 10 days, according to Weather Services Corp.
The Southwest was expected to see slightly below normal temperatures through Friday, but near normal temperatures were forecast for the next 6 to 10 days.

Bonneville Power Administration (BPA) continued to refrain from offering surplus power during morning and evening peaks on Friday, but lowered prices for shoulder hours on Friday by $6.00 per MWh to $24.00 for Northwest deliveries and $25.00 for California-Oregon border (COB) sales.
BPA also offered peak hour block sales for Saturday.
Firm, peak electricity at COB for Friday was quoted $25.00-28.00 per MWh, compared with $35.00-40.00 for Thursday.
Off-peak COB for Friday was slightly lower at $9.00-11.00.
Friday firm, peak power at Mid-Columbia (Mid-C) fell to $28.00-30.00, while off-peak was at $11.00-12.00.
Firm, peak Palo Verde (PV) electricity for Friday was quoted $26.00-30.00, while off-peak was at $10.00-11.00 per MWh.
Friday firm, peak prices at Four Corners were quoted at $24.00-28.00, while off-peak was at $10.00-11.00.
